criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and estate-level domestic water service access in Nairobi (piped utility connections, rationing, water pressure, continuity, supplementary tankers, boreholes, and water kiosks) across four middle-class estates in Langata and the Canaan slum-upgrading estate bordering Kibera.
criterion_notes.c2: Both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading are satisfied. Under the plain wording, the study examines how Kenya's constitutional human right to water, commercialized county-owned parastatal utility governance (Nairobi Water regulated by WASREB), and institutional fragmentation shape water access. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the study directly analyzes concrete administrative, discretionary, enforcement, and tariff/billing mechanisms governing service access: (1) institutional categorization into 'formal' versus 'Informal Region' utility offices and resulting administrative burden/deflection when Canaan's newly formalized residents report pipe tapping and are sent back and forth between offices; (2) street-level bureaucratic discretion and accommodation by utility actors (the Managing Director dispatching tankers upon personal pressure, distribution teams operating rationing valves, and utility plumbers installing unauthorized direct main-line connections for side payments to bypass rationing); (3) non-enforcement against illegal pipe diversions; and (4) formal cost-recovery and monthly service-fee/billing rules that strain low-income residents in Canaan.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative socio-legal empirical study based on 12 months of multi-sited ethnographic fieldwork in Nairobi (November 2021 to March 2024), employing semi-structured interviews, focus groups, participant observation with Nairobi Water field teams and residents, and analysis of a residential estate WhatsApp group. Per review rules, qualitative socio-legal studies with identifiable empirical methods are eligible for the systematic review and mechanism synthesis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative empirical outcomes on piped water service availability, continuity/reliability (days per week with water vs. weeks without supply), hydraulic pressure across floors and pipe branches, dry taps, and forced reliance on costly or laborious alternative water sources (kiosks in Kibera and private tankers).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (households, residential estates/committees in Langata and Canaan Estate, and street-level Nairobi Water employees in Nairobi, Kenya), exposure (formalized utility connection status, formal vs. informal regional office jurisdiction and administrative burden, street-level utility discretion/enforcement, and monthly billing), outcome (realized/concretized piped water continuity, pressure, and access), and study design (multi-sited ethnographic comparative case study) are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: An unreliable and sparse water supply in Nairobi’s piped grid means that a formal water connection does not always equal access to water.

The study is based on twelve months of ethnographic fieldwork conducted in Nairobi between November 2021 and March 2024. I have employed ethnographic methods such as semi-structured interviews, focus groups, and participant observation.

Although Canaan is officially a formal area, Nathaniel was told by this office to go to the office for the “Informal Region” in charge of informalized areas like Kibera, from where he was sent back again. In this way, the resident committee of Canaan has been unsuccessful in mobilizing the right people to establish their water claims, and the ambiguity of their formality status makes it easier for the officials to deflect Nathaniel’s complaints.

The most valuable relationships to mobilize in order to receive water seem to be with those who can manipulate the grid, such as plumbers and water service provider employees with knowledge of the valve system. This means that specific people rather than one institution grant people access to water, and the right to water becomes embedded in social relationships with these people.

Nathaniel, the vice-chair of the Canaan estate committee, expresses the irony of how, despite Canaan having a formal water connection, Kibera receives more water: “we have meters, but we are not getting water. And then the people from the informal area who don’t have meters are getting water more days than us who have meters”

raw_response.exposure: Legal and institutional formalization under Kenya's constitutional right to water and commercialized utility structure (Nairobi Water), administrative division and buck-passing between formal and Informal Region utility offices, street-level discretion and informal accommodation by utility management/plumbers/valve operators, non-enforcement against pipe diversions, and monthly cost-recovery billing.
raw_response.outcome: Actualized ('concretized') household and estate piped water supply availability, continuity/frequency (days per week of supply), hydraulic pressure, dry taps, and reliance on alternative water sources (water kiosks, boreholes, and private tankers).
raw_response.population_and_sample: Residents and estate committee members of four middle-class estates in Langata and the Canaan slum-upgrading estate bordering Kibera, plus Nairobi Water employees (southern region, leakage repair team, and Informal Region office) in Nairobi, Kenya, observed over 12 months of fieldwork (Nov 2021–Mar 2024; exact total interviewee count not reported).
raw_response.rationale: This qualitative socio-legal and multi-sited ethnographic study satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1–c6) for the systematic review. It empirically investigates why formal utility connections and Kenya's constitutional right to water fail to deliver reliable domestic water access in Nairobi, comparing four middle-class estates in Langata with the newly formalized Canaan slum-upgrading estate. Under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2, it examines concrete administrative and rule-type mechanisms governing service access—specifically administrative deflection between Nairobi Water's formal and 'Informal Region' offices, street-level discretion by utility managers, valve operators, and plumbers (including informal tanker dispatch and unauthorized main-line connections bypassing rationing), non-enforcement against pipe tapping, and monthly utility billing/cost-recovery rules—and links them to household and estate water continuity, pressure, and exclusion outcomes.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative multi-sited ethnographic comparative case study (semi-structured interviews, focus groups, participant observation, and WhatsApp group message analysis)
